title: TOP 15 Hanging Structures Even Engineers Can't Explain
fullText: Imagine you are standing on a wooden plank 30 cm wide bolted into a vertical cliff face 2,000 m above the ground. There is a rusted chain to hold on to. There is nothing below you for 400 m and the planks under your boots were installed by a dowist priest 700 years ago. People do this every single day. There is a cue to get on. Now look up because above you, scattered across this planet, there are buildings that should have fallen centuries ago and simply did not. There is a monastery in China held to a cliff by oak beams the width of your arm and it has been hanging there for 1,500 years. There is a church on top of a stone pillar 40 m tall where one man lived completely alone for two decades. There are coffins nailed to a cliff a 100 meters up by a people who were wiped off the map before anyone thought to ask them how they did it. These are the 15 most impossible hanging structures on Earth. Stay until the end because number one has survived earthquakes that cracked buildings in the valley below it. And engineers will tell you that the parts you can see holding it up are not holding it up at all. Some of them do not even touch the ground. And before we start, tell me in the comments where you are watching from right now. Last time, people from over 40 countries were watching at the same time. Let us see if you can beat that tonight. We start in Spain with houses that have been leaning out over a canyon since before Columbus sailed. Number 15, the hanging houses of Quanka. In the old city of Quanka, about 160 km east of Madrid, a row of medieval houses sits on the very lip of a limestone gorge. Their wooden balconies do not rest on the rock. They project out past the edge over open air held up by beams that run backward into the stone. The drop below is the War River Valley roughly 40 meters straight down. These houses date to the 15th century and there were once dozens of them running the entire length of the cliff. Most collapsed. Some were pulled down before they could. Three survive. The engineering is beautifully simple and that is exactly why it works. Horizontal timber beams are driven deep into the rock and anchored into the masonry behind. The balconies are cantalievered off the end of those beams. The weight of the house sitting behind pins the beam down. The way your hand holds down one end of a ruler while the other end sticks out over the edge of a table. It holds perfectly as long as nobody gets ambitious. Several owners across the centuries decided to add another floor or extend the balcony a little further out over the view. Every time that happened, the maths quietly stopped working. The load out front eventually exceeded the load behind and the beam pivoted. The three that survive are the three nobody improved. Those houses lean over a drop. The next structure does something considerably stranger. It hangs above a city upside down and it has been carrying 80,000 people a day since 1901. Number 14, the Whooper Tall Suspension Railway, Germany. In the German city of Vupertal, the trains do not run on the ground. They hang underneath a steel frame suspended 8 m above the streets and 12 m above the surface of the Whooper River and they have been doing it since 1901. The line runs for 13.3 km. It carries around 80,000 passengers a day. It is the oldest electric elevated railway with suspended carriages anywhere in the world and it is not a museum piece. It is the actual public transport system of the city. people take it to work. The reason it exists at all is that Vupertall sits in a narrow valley with almost no flat ground. There was no room for a conventional railway, no space for tracks, and no appetite for demolishing half the city to make some. So, the engineer Ouigen Langan proposed the obvious solution, which was to stop trying to put the railway on the ground and hang it over the river instead. The whole system rests on around 19,000 tons of steel carried by iron trestles, many of which are the original structures from the 1890s. And in 1950, a circus director had what he considered a magnificent idea. He would put a young elephant on the suspension railway, ride one stop, and generate a spectacular amount of free publicity. The elephant was called Tufi. Tufi was not consulted. She lasted a matter of seconds inside the carriage before panicking, charging the sidewall, breaking clean through it, and falling 12 m into the Vuper River. She survived, minor injuries only. Two passengers were hurt in the process. The circus director was prosecuted and fined. The newspapers had the best week of their lives, and Tufi became so beloved by the city that there is a statue of her there today. The railway itself was undamaged, which tells you something about how the Germans built things in 1898. That railway hangs over a city. The next town does the exact opposite. It lives underneath a rock that weighs more than every building in it combined. Number 13. Setil de las bodeas, Spain. In Andalucia, about 100 km from Seville, there is a town of roughly 3,000 people where entire streets have a ceiling. Not a roof, a ceiling. A single mass of basaltt projecting out over the road and the houses built directly underneath it. The rock is the roof. Many of these buildings have no upper structure of their own at all. There is a facade, a door, a couple of windows, and then the rest of the house simply continues backward into the cliff. People have been living under this overhang since the Neolithic, which means somebody looked at a giant unstable looking slab of rock several thousand years ago and thought that is a home. The town as it stands now dates to the 12th century. The logic is climate. Under the stone, the temperature holds steady, cool through Andelusian summers that regularly pass 40° C, warmer through winter with no heating and no cooling and no effort of any kind. The wine sellers that gave the town its name stayed at a constant temperature year round for free. The question every visitor asks within about 11 seconds of arriving is whether the rock is going to come down. Engineers have surveyed it repeatedly. It is stable. It has been stable for a very long time. It is one continuous mass rather than stacked layers and there is no evidence of progressive failure anywhere along it. which is a completely reassuring answer that helps absolutely nobody. Because if you sit at a table in one of those streets and look up, you are looking at several thousand tons of stone directly above your dinner. And no amount of geological surveying makes that feel like a normal place to eat. Number 12, the Husini hanging bridge, Pakistan. Northern Pakistan, the Hunza Valley. A rope bridge roughly 190 m long strung across the river. The planks are wooden. They are spaced far apart and a great many of them are missing entirely. Below is glacial meltwater moving fast enough that the current would kill you well before the cold got the chance. There is a second bridge running parallel to it. Older, half collapsed, still hanging in the wind. Nobody has taken it down. This is not an attraction. It is the crossing. Villages on the far side use it to reach everything. People carry goods across it. Children cross it to get to school. It sways violently in the wind. And it is designed [music] to because a rigid structure in that valley would tear its own anchors out within a season. It has been rebuilt many times. Same materials, same method, same people who need to get to the other side. That bridge is frightening because it barely exists. The next structure is frightening because of where somebody decided to put it. Number 11, Pjama Castle, Slovenia. About 50 km from Ljubljana, there is a castle built into the mouth of a cave halfway up a vertical cliff. 123 m high. It is important to be precise about this. It is not a castle beside a cave. The cliff forms the entire back wall and the roof. The front is four floors of masonry wedged into the opening like a cork. And behind that facade, the cave system keeps going for kilometers into the mountain. The site appears in records as early as 1202. The castle you see today was rebuilt in 1570. And its most famous occupant was a 15th century robber knight named Arazzim Luger who killed a relative of the Holy Roman Emperor and then retreated to the one building in Europe least convenient to attack. An imperial army came for him. A castle inside a cliff has exactly one weakness, which is that you cannot resupply it under siege. Except Arzom could. because a natural passage ran up through the cave system behind the castle and came out on the mountainside above, well outside the army's lines. The siege lasted over a year. The Imperial commander could not get in, could not starve him out, and could not work out why. Azam's response to this was to throw fresh cherries down at the soldiers camped below in the middle of a siege, in the wrong season for cherries. He was eventually killed by a single cannonball fired at the only part of the castle that projected out beyond the protection of the rock. At the exact moment a bribed servant signaled that Arasm was inside it. He was in the toilet. The toilet was on an outer wall because in a castle built inside a cliff, there is nowhere else on earth to put a toilet. The most defensible fortress in central Europe was brought down by plumbing and a servant with a lantern. That castle uses the cliff as its back wall. The next one uses the cliff as the floor, the wall, and the roof simultaneously 900 m above a valley. Number 10, Ostrog Monastery, Montenegro. Set into a near vertical rock face above the Zeta Valley at roughly 900 m, Ostrog Monastery is carved into the cliff and painted brilliant white so that seen from the valley floor, the mountain appears to have a light switched on inside it. It was founded in the 17th century by a bishop named Vasilier who came here to shelter in the caves and never left. There are two churches, both built inside natural cavities in the rock. The fresco inside them were painted directly onto the cave walls in the 1660s following the curve of the stone rather than any flat surface because there were no flat surfaces. The construction problem was brutal in its simplicity. There is no ledge, no shelf, no natural platform of any kind. Every stone, every beam, every bucket of lime, every liter of water had to be carried up a mountain path by hand and then assembled inside a cave mouth that sloped in three directions at once. Around a 100,000 pilgrims make the journey every year. A significant number walk the final stretch barefoot, which takes several hours. Four centuries later, the logistics have not changed at all. Everything that goes into Ostrog still comes up the same way it always did, carried by somebody, one load at a time. Ostrog holds one building against a cliff. The next place holds an entire village. And the village and the mountain are the same object. Number nine, Alhajara, Yemen. In the Har Mountains at more than 2,000 m above sea level, there is a village built in the 12th century where the stone towerhouses do not sit on top of the mountain. They appear to grow out of it. The builders used the exposed rock of the ridge itself as the foundation and the lower walls then continued upward and cut stone of exactly the same color quarried from the same ridge. The join is so precise that from any distance you genuinely cannot tell where the geology stops and the architecture begins. The village looks like the mountain decided to become a building. Some of these houses are six and seven stories tall. They stand directly on the edge of a drop of several hundred meters. There are no terraces, no setbacks, no margin of safety, no railings. In some of these homes, the outer wall of the living room is the cliff face. The placement was defensive. Alhajara was built as a fortress village, and taking it would have meant climbing a mountain under fire from seven stories above. What engineers find genuinely remarkable is not the height. It is that these are dry stone structures built without modern mortar in a region with almost no timber available to reinforce anything on an exposed ridge in a seismically active part of the world. They have stood through 800 years of wind, sun, rain, and earthquake. The stone is doing every bit of the work purely through the accuracy with which each block was cut to sit against the next one. They have been standing since before England had a parliament and nobody has needed to fix them. Number eight, the cliff chambers of Bandandyara, Mali. Start with what is inside them. In the mud chamber set into the Bandiagara escarment, archaeologists have found human remains that are more than 700 years old and are not skeletons. They are bodies desiccated by the dry heat, wrapped in woven cotton textiles that still hold their color and their pattern. Buried with wooden headrests and iron jewelry and leather, the textiles are among the oldest surviving woven cloth in West Africa. They survived because the chambers are so high, so dry, and so completely sealed off from everything that nothing has ever reached them. Not water, not animals, not people. The escarment runs for 150 km across central Mali, rising as high as 500 m. Set into that cliff face at heights that require ropes and serious climbing to reach are hundreds of small mud structures with conicle roofs, graneries, and burial chambers. And the Doon people who live below the escarment today did not build them. They were built by a people called the Telm who occupied these cliffs from around the 11th century and had disappeared by the 16th. The Doon arrived and found the structures already there, already ancient, already impossible to reach. The construction question is not academic. Mud has to be mixed with water. Water is extraordinarily heavy. The nearest reliable source is at the base of the escarment. Some of these chambers sit in the rock face with no path, no ledge, and no plausible route for a person carrying anything at all, let alone enough wet clay to build a room. The Doon explanation recorded by ethnographers who worked in the region in the 20th century is that the Telm could fly. The more likely reality is that the escarment was forested when the Telm lived here. Trees and vines against the cliff would have provided access that vanished as the climate dried and the forest died back. But that is an inference. It is not a record. The Telm left no writing and the last person who knew how it was done died about 500 years ago. They built into the cliff for safety and they succeeded so completely that nobody could follow them up. Then they disappeared anyway. And the only thing left of them is a few hundred rooms full of preserved bodies in cloth that nobody can climb up to. If you have made it this far, you are exactly the kind of person this channel was built for. Subscribe so the next one finds you. Those chambers hold the dead. The next cliff held an entire town and it was emptied out in a single generation for reasons nobody has settled. Number seven, Cliff Palace, Mesa Verde, Colorado. Under a sandstone overhang in southwestern Colorado, there is a village of 150 rooms and 23 ceremonial chambers built by ancestral puebloans between roughly 1190 and 1280 of the common era. About 100 people lived in it. The whole structure sits inside a natural al cove which means the rock above is the roof and the rock behind is the back wall. Everything else, every sandstone block, every bucket of mortar, every roof beam was carried up. Access was not by staircase because there was no staircase. Residents climbed hand and tow holds cut directly into the cliff face, some of which you can still see today. They did this carrying water, carrying firewood, carrying food, carrying children. The al cove does something that the builders very obviously understood. In winter, when the sun sits low in the sky, light reaches all the way to the back wall and warms the stone through the day. In summer, when the sun is high, the overhang shades the entire village completely. It is passively heated and cooled by nothing but the angle of the rock above it. 800 years before anyone used the phrase passive solar design, and within roughly a century of being finished, it was empty. The residents did not destroy it. They did not burn it. They left it standing, walked south, and never came back. A prolonged drought is the leading explanation, but it has never been fully settled, and the pace of the departure across the whole region still puzzles archaeologists. It sat there in perfect condition, protected by the same overhang that had sheltered its residents for 600 years. In 1888, two ranchers named Richard Weather and Charlie Mason were riding through a snowstorm looking for stray cattle. They came to the edge of a canyon, looked across through the falling snow, and saw a city in the opposite wall. That town was found by accident. The next path was built on purpose by one man, and nobody can explain how he started. Number six, the plank walk of Mount Hua, China. Mount Hua in Shani province rises to 2,154 meters. On the south face, at a point where the rock stops sloping and simply goes vertical, there is a path made of wooden boards bolted into the cliff. The boards are around 30 cm wide. In several sections, the planks run out altogether and the route becomes a line of shallow footholds chipped into the stone with a chain to hold. You are 400 meters above the nearest thing that could be described as ground. It was built roughly 700 years ago by a Dowist priest named Hao Datong who wanted to reach a hermitage near the peak. It was never intended for visitors. It was built for a small number of monks who considered the difficulty of the journey to be the entire point of the journey. Today it is open to the public. There is a harness system which was added relatively recently. Before that, people simply walked it with nothing. But here is the part that stops engineers. To bolt a wooden plank into a vertical rock wall 400 m up, somebody has to already be there. Hanging with tools, drilling into stone, working with both hands on a surface with no ledge, no platform, and nothing whatsoever to stand on. Which means the first person up did it with no planks at all. just rope anchored somewhere above and the decision to go over the edge. There is no record of who went first. There is no record of how many attempts it took or what happened to the attempts that failed. Number five, the hanging coffins of the bow, China. Gong Xien County, Sichuan Province. wooden coffins fixed to vertical cliff faces, some of them nearly a 100 meters above the ground, resting on wooden stakes hammered horizontally into the rock or wedged into natural crevices. More than a hundred are still up there. There were once many, many more. They were placed by the Bow people, an ethnic group who lived in this region for centuries. Most of the surviving coffins date to the Ming dynasty, though the practice itself goes back much further. The bow believed that the dead belonged at height, closer to the spirits, above the reach of animals, of floods, and of enemies. Each coffin is carved from a single hollowed hardwood log. They weigh 200 kg and more. They had to be raised up a sheer cliff, maneuvered into position on stakes barely wider than a wrist, and secured by people working with rope, timber, and no metal machinery of any kind. And then in the 1570s, the bow were destroyed. The Ming Imperial Court launched a military campaign against them. It was not a battle for territory. It was an extermination. Contemporary Chinese records describe the systematic killing of the bow, the burning of their settlements, and the hunting down of survivors across the mountains. Those who lived scattered into other populations and stopped calling themselves B because to be identified as B was to be killed. Within a few years, a people who had lived in those mountains for over a thousand years no longer existed. The coffins stayed exactly where they were. Nobody came to maintain them. Nobody came to add to them. The wooden stakes went on holding 200 kg of hardwood against a vertical cliff for 450 years for a culture that had been erased in a valley where nobody was left who could read the paintings beside them. Archaeologists have proposed scaffolding built up from the base. They have proposed lowering the coffins from the clifftop on ropes. They have proposed earthn ramps later removed. All three are plausible. None of them has ever been demonstrated. And there is no one to ask because the Ming army made certain of that. The coffins are the only sentence the bow left behind and it is written in a language that died with them. Those coffins hold the dead. The next structure held one living man alone for 20 years. Number four, the Katsky pillar, Georgia. In central Georgia, a limestone monolith rises 40 m straight out of a green valley floor. It is not part of a ridge. It is not attached to a mountain. It stands entirely alone with vertical walls on every side and a flat top the size of a small garden. And on top of it, there is a church. The structures up there date to around the 9th or 10th century. For most of the last thousand years, nobody [clears throat] went up. Locals called it the pillar of life, treated it as sacred, and left it completely alone. which meant that for centuries the top of that rock was a place people could see every day of their lives and never visit. Nobody knew what was on it. The first documented modern ascent was in 1944 by a team led by the mountaineer Alexander Japarid. What they found on the summit was the ruin of a small chapel, a burial crypt, and a wine celler. Then in the 1990s, a Georgian man named Maxim Karadz decided to live up there. He had been a crane operator. Then he had gone to prison. Then he became a monk. He restored the chapel on top of the pillar and he stayed on it for roughly 20 years. Access was by an iron ladder bolted to the side of the rock. A climb of about 20 minutes. Food and supplies came up by winch. He came down twice a week to speak with people at the base. And then he climbed back up and pulled his life up behind him. Building that chapel in the 10th century meant getting stone, mortar, timber, and water up 40 meters of sheer limestone. There is no account of how it was done because the people who did it never expected anyone to ask. What we do know is that once it was finished, it was left alone so completely for so long that it dropped out of history entirely and had to be found again by climbers with modern equipment. That pillar holds a chapel. The next monastery is a whole complex built inside the mouth of a cave and for four months of the year the only way to reach it is to walk up a frozen river. Number three, Fugtal Monastery, India. In the Zanscar region of Leidda in the Indian Himalayas, a monastery is built into the opening of an enormous natural cave in a cliff face at roughly 3,800 m. The buildings are stacked into the cave mouth in a honeycomb of mud brick and timber layered upward and outward so that the entire complex looks like a wasp nest fixed to the side of a mountain. Around 70 monks live there. There is no road. There has never been a road. Every beam, every brick, every sack of barley, every book in its library was carried in by hand or by horse along a mountain trail. And in winter that trail becomes impassible which leaves one route. The Zanscar River freezes solid and people walk on it for days in temperatures well below minus20° C along a frozen river at the bottom of a gorge carrying supplies on their backs. The route has a name. They call it the Chadar, which means the sheet. The ice is not uniform. Sections give way. Travelers carry poles to test it and they sleep in caves along the bank. The monastery was founded in the 12th century. Inside the cave, there is a spring that has been flowing continuously for as long as anyone has recorded. It does not increase in the monsoon and it does not decrease in the dry season. It provides all the water for the entire community, which is the only reason a monastery in that position is possible at all. Conservators who have studied the structure have reached a conclusion that sounds backwards. The reason a mud and timber building has survived 800 years in an earthquake zone at high altitude is precisely that it is mud and timber. The joints flex, the walls move. A concrete structure in the same place would have cracked and failed generations ago. Fugtal is built into one cliff. The next place has monasteries on top of six separate rock towers. And for 600 years, the only way up was to sit in a net and hope. Number two, Meteora, Greece. In central Greece, a cluster of sandstone pillars erupts out of the flat vessel plane. Some of them stand more than 300 m tall with vertical sides and flat summits. From the 14th century onward, monks built monasteries on top of them. At the peak, there were 24. Six remain active today. The construction problem here is the purest on this entire list because there was nothing. No path, no stairs, no route of any kind. And in many places, the pillars actually overhang, meaning the rock curves outward as you go up. So, a rope dropped from the summit hangs in midair without ever touching the wall. The first monks climbed using removable ladders lashed together in sections and scaffolding wedged into cracks in the stone. Then they hauled everything else up behind them. Building stone, roof tiles, timber, food, water, other monks. Once a monastery was finished, the standard method of arrival for roughly 600 years was to sit in a rope net and be winched up by hand from a windless at the top. Visitors wrote about this experience and the accounts share a common feature which is that everybody asked the same question on the way up. They asked how often the rope was replaced. The answer that comes down to us recorded by more than one traveler was that the rope was replaced when the Lord let it break. Stairs were finally cut into the rock in the 1920s. Before that, these monasteries were effectively unreachable, and that was not a side effect. It was the design brief. They were built during a period of Ottoman expansion, specifically so that no army could get to them. No army ever did. Number one, the hanging monastery of Hang Shan, China. In Shani province, in a narrow gorge below Mount Hang, there is a temple attached to a vertical rock wall about 75 m above the canyon floor. 40 halls and pavilions connected by wooden walkways and staircases barely wide enough for one person. The entire complex projecting out from the cliff face on horizontal beams. It was founded around the year 491 of the common era. It has been hanging there for more than 1,500 years. Now look at any photograph of it and you will see dozens of slender wooden poles running down from the walkways toward the rock below. Apparently propping the whole thing up. They look exactly like what is keeping the monastery in the air. They are not carrying the building. They never were. The actual load is taken by oak cross beams driven horizontally into sockets cut deep into the cliff. The beams were treated with tongue oil, which swells the timber and expands it hard against the walls of the socket, wedging it in place under permanent pressure. The deeper the beam sits, the tighter it grips, and the weight of the structure above increases the friction inside the socket instead of pulling the beam out. The building holds itself up by pressing itself in. The vertical poles were added later. Some sources describe them as supplementary support. Others are blunter and say they were put there because visitors flatly refused to walk onto a temple that appeared to be attached to nothing. Several of those poles do not carry any load at all. On some of them, you can slide a sheet of paper underneath and pull it out the other side. And then there is the sight selection which is the other half of the reason it survived. The monastery sits inside a recess under an overhang. That overhang keeps direct rain off the timber, keeps direct sun off it, and shields it from the worst of the wind funneling through the gorge. The canyon floor below floods, and the monastery sits well above the flood line. The mountains on either side restrict direct sunlight to roughly 3 hours a day, which is precisely why 1500-year-old wood has not rotted. It has been through earthquakes strong enough to damage buildings in the valley. A rigid structure would have sheared at the anchor points. This one moves. The joints flex, the beams shift inside their sockets, and it settles back. It is also the only temple in China that houses Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism together under one roof. Three religions side by side, 75 m up on beams hammered into a cliff by people who had no steel, no concrete, no cranes, and who left behind not one single drawing of what they were doing or why they were confident it would work. 1,500 years, 40 halls, 75 m of air underneath. And the poles you can see are not the ones holding it up. 15 structures hanging off the side of this planet. Medieval balconies over a Spanish gorge. And the ones that fell were the ones somebody improved. A railway that has carried a city upside down since 1901 and once dropped an elephant into a river. A town with a ceiling of solid rock. A rope bridge with missing planks that children still cross to reach school. A castle in a cave mouth beaten by a cannonball and a bathroom. A white monastery burning against a Montenegron cliff. A Yemeni village that grew out of the mountain it stands on. Chambers in Mali full of bodies wrapped in cloth that still holds its color. Built by people whose neighbors said they could fly. 50 rooms sealed in a Colorado cliff for six centuries and found by two men chasing cows in a snowstorm. A plank path bolted to a vertical face by somebody who had to hang there to build it. Coffins raised 100 m by a people the Ming dynasty erased before anyone asked how. A church on a lone pillar where one man lived by himself for 20 years. A monastery reachable in winter only by walking up a frozen river. Six monasteries on top of towers reached by rope net for 600 years replaced [music] when the Lord let them break and a temple hanging on oiled oak beams since the year 491. Here is what strikes me about all of this. Almost none of these were built to impress anyone. They were built by people who needed to be somewhere unreachable for safety, for solitude, or simply because the flat ground had run out and there was nowhere else left to go. The impossibility was never the point. It was just the cheapest option available at the time. Which one would you actually set foot on? Tell me in the comments. And if you made it all the way here, you already know this channel was built for people exactly like you. Hit subscribe, turn on notifications. The next video takes you somewhere even more impossible. We will see you there.
fullTextVi: Hãy tưởng tượng bạn đang đứng trên một tấm ván gỗ rộng 30 cm được bắt vít vào mặt vách đá thẳng đứng cách mặt đất 2.000 m. Có một sợi dây xích rỉ sét để bám vào. Không có gì bên dưới bạn trong 400 m và những tấm ván dưới ủng của bạn đã được một linh mục theo chủ nghĩa Dowist lắp đặt cách đây 700 năm. Mọi người làm điều này mỗi ngày. Có một gợi ý để tiếp tục. Bây giờ hãy tra cứu vì phía trên bạn, rải rác khắp hành tinh này, có những tòa nhà lẽ ra đã sụp đổ từ nhiều thế kỷ trước nhưng đơn giản là không. Có một tu viện ở Trung Quốc được giữ trên một vách đá bằng dầm gỗ sồi rộng bằng cánh tay của bạn và nó đã được treo ở đó suốt 1.500 năm. Có một nhà thờ nằm ​​trên đỉnh cột đá cao 40 m một người đàn ông sống hoàn toàn một mình trong hai thập kỷ. Có những chiếc quan tài được người dân đóng đinh vào vách đá cao 100m những người đã bị xóa khỏi bản đồ trước khi có người kịp hỏi thăm họ thế nào đã làm nó. Đây là 15 cấu trúc treo bất khả thi nhất trên Trái đất. Ở lại đến cuối cùng vì số một đã sống sót sau trận động đất làm nứt các tòa nhà ở thung lũng bên dưới nó. Và các kỹ sư sẽ cho bạn biết rằng những bộ phận bạn có thể nhìn thấy đang giữ nó không hề giữ nó chút nào. Một số trong số họ thậm chí không chạm đất.
